choices.text: United SFO-DEN-BNA, departing 1:55 p.m. and arriving 8:35 p.m. with a 75-minute connection; standard-economy seat selection is deferred until online check-in.
Delta SFO-SLC-BNA, departing 2:00 p.m. and arriving 8:40 p.m. with a 78-minute connection; free window seats are selectable now on both legs.
American SFO-DFW-BNA, departing 2:05 p.m. and arriving 8:45 p.m. with an 80-minute connection; free window seats are selectable now on both legs.
Alaska SFO-SEA-BNA, departing 1:50 p.m. and arriving 8:30 p.m. with a 77-minute connection; free window seats are selectable now on both legs.

probes.difficulty_rationale: Without history, the small timing differences, carrier choice, and immediate-seat availability have no universal ordering. The label requires applying both the window preference's seat-location-only boundary and the competing soft United preference without allowing either to override a material itinerary difference.
probes.gold_action: Lead with the comparable United itinerary, explicitly note that seat selection is deferred, and request a window immediately when online check-in opens rather than changing carriers solely for a currently selectable window.
probes.label_rationale: The options are deliberately comparable on fare, departure period, arrival, and connection quality. Jonah has specifically said to take a window if available but not let it decide the carrier, while United remains a soft positive tie-breaker among otherwise suitable flights. A therefore leads; its deferred seat-selection limitation should be recorded and followed up at check-in rather than treated as a reason to switch airlines for a window.
probes.query: Jonah is traveling solo from SFO to Nashville on Monday for a Tuesday 10:00 a.m. training. All times are local. Every option is regular economy, costs $426, has one comfortable connection, departs in the afternoon, arrives between 8:30 and 8:45 p.m., and permits normal hotel check-in. Which line should lead the shortlist?

choices.text: Add the $38 preferred-seat bundle now and lock a window immediately.
Keep the selected standard fare, record that seat selection is deferred, and at online check-in request a free window first; use an aisle only if no acceptable window remains.
Keep the selected standard fare but add no seating follow-up, accepting whatever automatic assignment is made later.
Move to the later-arriving Delta alternative solely because it permits a free window selection now.

probes.difficulty_rationale: The query alone leaves the value of immediate certainty, a $38 add-on, a later arrival, and a check-in task unresolved. History is needed to combine Jonah's free-window tendency with the specific rule for deferred seat selection rather than assuming either that he should pay now or that automatic assignment is sufficient.
probes.gold_action: Keep the selected fare, document the deferred seat-selection limitation, and seek a free window at the earliest available check-in time, with an aisle only as a fallback if no acceptable window remains.
probes.label_rationale: Jonah has repeatedly treated a window as a request to make when seat selection opens, while declining to pay merely for that seat. B preserves the already suitable itinerary and price, makes the required follow-up explicit, and does not silently abandon the window request. A trades money for immediate certainty, C trades the requested follow-up for convenience, and D reopens the itinerary solely for seat availability.
probes.query: Jonah has chosen a solo Monday SFO-to-Kansas City work flight because its fare and timing meet the trip needs. The standard-economy fare is $404. Its airline says the standard seat map will remain unavailable until online check-in opens 24 hours before departure; a $38 preferred-seat bundle would unlock immediate seat selection. A same-fare Delta alternative has a free window selectable now but arrives at the hotel 55 minutes later. He has no companion seating need and has given no current instruction to buy a seat product. Which booking instruction should be attached?

choices.text: Seats 18B and 18C: adjacent middle and aisle seats together.
Seats 18A and 18F: a window seat for each traveler, but on opposite sides of the cabin and not together.
Seats 10A and 10C: one window and one aisle on the same side, with an unrelated passenger seated between them.
Seats 14C and 15D: two aisle seats in adjacent rows, so each traveler has aisle access but they are not side-by-side.

probes.difficulty_rationale: A and B present a genuine personal tradeoff between adjacent seating and two window seats, with C and D offering other plausible individual-seat benefits. There is no generic answer from the query alone; the label depends on applying the companion exception instead of overgeneralizing the solo window preference.
probes.gold_action: Accept the adjacent 18B and 18C pair, prioritizing seating together over obtaining a separate window seat.
probes.label_rationale: The normal window default is scoped to solo travel and yields to a companion seating need. Across several personal trips, Jonah explicitly placed being together ahead of either a window or aisle. A is the only option that keeps the pair adjacent; B, C, and D offer individual seat-location advantages only by separating them.
probes.query: Jonah and his spouse are flying together for a four-hour personal-weekend flight. Their tickets, cabin, and fare are already fixed, and all of the following seat holds are free. They have no mobility needs, no tight connection, and no current seat instruction. Which hold should be accepted before the seat map hold expires?
